en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Twenty, Mātaṅga Chapter
12. The Jātaka of the Five Wise Men “Five wise men have come together;
a question occurs to me—listen to it!”
“Who indeed would reveal a secret matter,
whether it concerns one who deserves blame or one who deserves praise?
“You, O protector of the earth, reveal it.”
"O Lord, you say that you are capable of bearing the burden;
having thoroughly examined your desires and inclinations,
O Ruler of Men, the five wise ones will then speak."
“She who is virtuous, not fickle,
obedient to her husband’s will and pleasing;
whether there is something blameworthy or praiseworthy— ”
One may reveal a secret matter to one’s wife.
He who is a refuge, a destination, and a final resort for one who has fallen into distress and is afflicted—
One might praise what is blameworthy,
or reveal a secret matter to a friend.
"The eldest, the middle, and the youngest— "
But one who is established in virtue, concentrated, and firm in self,
may reveal a hidden matter— whether it be blameworthy or praiseworthy—
as if it were his own brother’s.
“He who follows the path of his father’s heart,
born after his father in peerless wisdom— he,
whether censuring what is blameworthy or praising what is praiseworthy, [is truly a son].”
She would reveal his secret matter.
"O best among two-legged beings, she is your mother,
who nourishes you with her own will and love."
One should reveal a secret matter even to one who is blameworthy or to one who is praiseworthy,
as one would to one's mother. For it is better that a secret remain a secret.
For it is not praised to disclose what is secret;
a wise person should endure the state of being unaccomplished,
but once accomplished, he may speak as he pleases.
“Why are you dejected, O best of kings?
We hear these words from you, O lord of bipeds:
‘With what thought are you sorrowful?’”
“Surely, O King, there is some transgression on my part.
“The wise Mahosadha is to be executed for his answers,” so was the one of vast intelligence commanded by me for execution.
“Reflecting on this, I am dejected;
for there is indeed no fault in you, O Queen.
“Now, when it is past midnight, you shall come.”
"What have you heard that your mind fears?
Who said what to you, O one of vast wisdom?
Pray, let us hear your words; tell us this."
“O Lord of Men, if it was your counsel that ‘Mahosadha is to be executed for his answers,’ yet he spoke in private with his wife— ”
"This which was heard by me has been made manifest from what was hidden:
that Senaka, while in the Sāla grove,
committed an evil deed that was utterly unworthy."
O Lord of Men, this secret which was told to me by my friend in private, when she revealed it to me,
I have now heard from you, O Pukkusa.
A disease arose that was not fit for kings;
having gone into seclusion, I told it to my brother.
This secret, which had been kept hidden, has now been heard by me.
"This is a distressing and unseemly affliction," said the Lord of Desire to the God of Men when he was touched by it,
as he spoke to his son in private.
This was heard by me as something hidden that has now been revealed:
that Sakka gave you that sublime eight-bent-jointed jewel, O Grandfather.
Today the King of the Devas has come into his hand;
having gone into seclusion, he spoke it to his mother.
This secret, which was made manifest, has been heard by me.
For it is better that what is secret remain secret,
for the disclosure of a secret is not praised;
a wise person should endure the state of being unaccomplished.
Once it has been accomplished, one may speak as one pleases.
One should not disclose a secret matter,
but guard it like a treasure.
For a wise person, it is not good to reveal a secret matter;
one should not disclose a secret to a woman.
The wise man [guards himself] from an enemy;
so too does the man who is restrained by material things and who holds his heart in check.
That man who awakens another person to a secret matter that has not yet been understood,
out of fear of the disclosure of his counsel—
Being like a servant, he endures.
As many as there are who know the secrets and counsels for the sake of a man’s welfare;
He has as many misfortunes as [he reveals];
therefore, he should not disclose what is secret.
He should speak in private during the day, keeping it confidential.
One should not utter speech excessively at night;
for eavesdroppers hear the counsel,
and therefore that counsel quickly leads to division.
The Twelfth Jātaka: The Birth Story of the Five Wise Men.
